items.t: Moderate to severe pain.

src.q: Treatment of moderate to severe pain.

items.t: MHRA (2025): prolonged-release opioids should not be used for acute pain after surgery; use immediate-release opioids for short-term post-operative pain.

src.q: prolonged-release opioids provide relief from chronic severe pain, however, they should not be used for the treatment of acute pain following surgery

items.t: Not for use in narcotic withdrawal treatment; not a substitute in opioid-dependent patients.

src.q: for use in narcotic withdrawal treatment
Tramadol is not suitable as a substitute in opioid-dependent patients.

items.t: Acute pain (adults and 12 years and over): initial 100 mg, then 50 or 100 mg every 4-6 hours; match duration to clinical need. Maximum 400 mg/day except in special circumstances.

src.q: Acute pain: An initial dose of 100 mg is usually necessary. This can be followed by doses of 50 or 100 mg 4-6 hourly intervals
The total daily dose of 400 mg active substance should not be exceeded, except in special circumstances.

items.t: Pain with chronic conditions: start 50 mg, then titrate to pain severity; reassess need regularly (dependence and withdrawal reported). Maximum 400 mg/day.

src.q: Pain associated with chronic conditions: An initial dose of 50 mg is advised and then titration according to pain severity.

items.t: Prolonged-release (adults and over 12 years): usually 100 mg twice daily (morning and evening); increase to 150 mg or 200 mg twice daily if needed. Interval at least 8 hours. Maximum 400 mg/day except in special clinical circumstances.

src.q: The starting dose is usually 100 mg tramadol hydrochloride as prolonged-release tablet twice daily, in the morning and in the evening. If the pain relief is not sufficient, the dose may be increased to 150 mg twice daily or 200 mg twice daily.
A total daily dose of 400 mg of tramadol hydrochloride should not be exceeded except in special clinical circumstances.
The dose interval must not be less than 8 hours.

items.t: Elderly: no adjustment usually needed up to 75 years without hepatic or renal insufficiency; over 75 years extend the dosing interval if necessary.

src.q: A dose adjustment is not usually necessary in patients up to 75 years without clinically manifest hepatic or renal insufficiency.
Therefore, if necessary the dosage interval is to be extended according to the patient's requirements.

items.t: Use the lowest effective dose; never longer than absolutely necessary. Agree goals and an end-of-treatment plan; taper gradually when stopping.

src.q: Tramadol should under no circumstances be administered for longer than absolutely necessary.
When a patient no longer requires therapy with tramadol, it may be advisable to taper the dose gradually to prevent symptoms of withdrawal.

items.t: Not suitable for children under 12 years (capsules and prolonged-release tablets).

src.q: Tramadol capsules are not suitable for children below the age of 12 years.
Tramadol prolonged-release tablets are not suitable for children under 12 years of age.

items.t: Post-operative use after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy for obstructive sleep apnoea: rare life-threatening events; extreme caution and close monitoring. Not recommended where respiratory function may be compromised.

src.q: Extreme caution should be exercised when tramadol is administered to children for post-operative pain relief
Tramadol is not recommended for use in children in whom respiratory function might be compromised

items.t: Hypersensitivity; acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, opioids or other psychotropic medicines; MAOI now or within 14 days; epilepsy not adequately controlled; narcotic withdrawal treatment.

src.q: in acute intoxication with alcohol, hypnotics, analgesics, opioids, or other psychotropic medicinal products
in patients who are receiving MAO inhibitors or who have taken them within the last 14 days
in patients with epilepsy not adequately controlled by treatment

items.t: Particular caution: opioid dependence, head injury, shock, reduced consciousness of uncertain origin, respiratory centre or function disorders, raised intracranial pressure (MR SmPC also: renal and hepatic impairment).

src.q: Tramadol may only be used with particular caution in opioid-dependent patients, patients with head injury, shock, a reduced level of consciousness of uncertain origin, disorders of the respiratory centre or function, increased intracranial pressure.

items.t: Seizures reported at recommended doses; higher risk above 400 mg/day or with other seizure-threshold-lowering medicines. Epilepsy or seizure susceptibility: only if compelling circumstances.

src.q: Convulsions have been reported in patients receiving tramadol at the recommended dose levels.
Patients with epilepsy or those susceptible to seizures should be only treated with tramadol if there are compelling circumstances.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome (alone or with serotonergic medicines): observe carefully at start and dose increases; reduce or stop if suspected.

src.q: Serotonin syndrome, a potentially life-threatening condition, has been reported in patients receiving tramadol in combination with other serotonergic agents or tramadol alone
If serotonin syndrome is suspected, a dose reduction or discontinuation of therapy should be considered depending on the severity of the symptoms.

items.t: Tolerance, dependence and opioid use disorder can develop even at therapeutic doses; higher risk with personal/family history of substance use disorder, tobacco use or mental health disorders. Monitor for drug-seeking behaviour.

src.q: Repeated use of Tramadol can lead to opioid use disorder (OUD).
Patients will require monitoring for signs of drug-seeking behaviour (e.g. too early requests for refills).

items.t: CYP2D6: poor metabolisers may get inadequate analgesia; ultra-rapid metabolisers risk opioid toxicity even at usual doses.

src.q: If a patient has a deficiency or is completely lacking this enzyme an adequate analgesic effect may not be obtained.
if the patient is an ultra-rapid metaboliser there is a risk of developing <side effects> of opioid toxicity even at commonly prescribed doses

items.t: Opioids may occasionally cause reversible adrenal insufficiency requiring monitoring and glucocorticoid replacement.

src.q: Opioid analgesics may occasionally cause reversible adrenal insufficiency requiring monitoring and glucocorticoid replacement therapy.

items.t: Sleep-related breathing disorders (central sleep apnoea): consider reducing the opioid dose.

src.q: In patients who present with CSA, consider decreasing the total opioid dosage.

items.t: SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, mirtazapine and MAOIs: serotonin syndrome risk. SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics, antipsychotics and other seizure-threshold-lowering drugs: convulsion risk.

src.q: Concomitant therapeutic use of tramadol and serotonergic medicinal products, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), MAO inhibitors (see section 4.3), tricyclic antidepressants and mirtazapine may cause serotonin syndrome
Tramadol can induce convulsions and increase the potential for selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs)

items.t: Warfarin and other coumarins: increased INR with major bleeding and bruising reported. Use caution; MHRA advises considering extra INR monitoring when starting tramadol and warning patients about bleeding signs.

src.q: Caution should be exercised during concomitant treatment with tramadol and coumarin derivatives (e.g. warfarin) due to reports of increased INR with major bleeding and ecchymoses in some patients.
consider whether additional monitoring of INR is required when starting tramadol or another concomitant medicine

items.t: Benzodiazepines, other opioids, other CNS depressants and alcohol: sedation, respiratory depression, coma and death; lowest dose, shortest duration if combined.

src.q: if a decision is made to prescribe tramadol concomitantly with respiratory or CNS depressants, the lowest effective dose of tramadol should be used, and the duration of the concomitant treatment should be as short as possible

items.t: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g. ketoconazole, ritonavir, erythromycin) might inhibit tramadol metabolism; clinical importance not studied.

src.q: Other medicinal products known to inhibit CYP3A4, such as ketoconazole, ritonavir and erythromycin, might inhibit the metabolism of tramadol
The clinical importance of such an interaction has not been studied

src.q: Simultaneous or previous administration of carbamazepine (enzyme inducer) may reduce the analgesic effect and shorten the duration of action.
The concomitant use of Tramadol with gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin) may result in respiratory depression, hypotension, profound sedation, coma or death.

items.t: St John's wort (THR SPC): reduced tramadol blood levels with risk of therapeutic failure; do not take together.

src.q: Analgesics Tramadol Reduced blood levels with risk Do not take with this product.

src.q: concomitant treatment of ciprofloxacin with drugs known to trigger seizures or lower the seizure threshold, such as but not limited to tramadol, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, should be avoided

items.t: Clopidogrel (clopidogrel SmPC): opioid agonists may delay and reduce clopidogrel absorption (clinical relevance unknown); in acute coronary syndrome consider a parenteral antiplatelet agent.

items.t: SmPCs: inadequate human safety evidence, so tramadol should not be used in pregnant women. Regular use may cause neonatal withdrawal; use in labour may depress neonatal breathing.

src.q: There is inadequate evidence available on the safety of tramadol in human pregnancy. Therefore tramadol should not be used in pregnant women.
Administration during labour may depress respiration in the neonate

items.t: BUMPS (differs from SmPC): take only if recommended by a doctor; studies overall do not show miscarriage or birth defects; use near delivery can cause neonatal withdrawal.

src.q: Tramadol should only be taken during pregnancy if recommended by your doctor.
Studies of pregnant women using tramadol do not, overall, show that it causes miscarriage or birth defects in the baby.

items.t: SPS: reserve tramadol in pregnancy for when other analgesics have been ineffective.

src.q: Reserve tramadol use in pregnancy where other alternative analgesics have been ineffective.

src.q: Tramadol (both oral and intravenous) can be used short-term during breastfeeding with caution and infant monitoring.
